chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn Yahya al-Khuzai'i, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from 'Asim ibn Yunus, from a man, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

He said to a man: 'With what do you treat your feverish one when he has fever?' He said: 'May Allah improve you, with these bitter medicines — safayaj, and al-ghafith, and what is similar to them.' So he said: 'Glory be to Allah, the One Who has the power to cure with the bitter, has the power to cure with the sweet.'

Then he said: 'When one of you has a fever, let him take a clean vessel, place a piece of sugar and a half in it, then recite over it what of the Quran is presentable to him. Then he places it under the stars, and places iron upon it. So when it is morning, he pours water over it and mixes it with his hand, then drinks it. So when it is the second night, he adds another piece of sugar so it becomes two and a half. So when it is the third night, he adds another piece of sugar so it becomes three and a half.'

key_terms.تَحْتَ النُّجُوم: Under the stars (exposed to the night sky)
key_terms.سُكَّرَة: Piece of sugar / lump of sugar
key_terms.مَحْمُوم: Feverish person / one suffering from fever

ai.seo_question: What is the recommended ritual remedy for fever according to Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) contrasts the conventional use of bitter medicines with the divine omnipotence that heals through both bitter and sweet, emphasizing that cure is by Allah's will. He prescribes a specific ritual remedy involving sugar, Quranic recitation, exposure to the night sky with iron, and a gradual increase of sugar over three nights, reflecting the Shia tradition of combining physical treatment (al-tibb al-jismani) with spiritual means (al-tibb al-ruhani).
